name: Umber Brown
lede: Umber brown is a dark, reddish chestnut brown, number 102 in Patrick Syme's colour chart, named for the earth pigment that painters used for shadows.

sections.title: From the paint box to the chart
sections.body:
Syme's chart of 1814 and 1821 borrowed freely from artists' supplies [3]. Baty observes that many of his terms came from painters' pigments and dyes, and that umber brown stands beside gamboge, Sienna yellow, sap green and lake red in that group; Syme probably used the real materials to make his swatches [3]. Several of the same names turn up in the flower-painting manuals of Brookshaw and Francia [3].

The pigment word is old. *Umber* comes from the Latin *ombra*, shadow, and it names a pigment useful for rendering shadows [4]. The pigment has its own article at [[umber]], with [[raw-umber]] and [[burnt-umber]] beside it; roasting umber drives water out of its iron hydroxides and gives the warm reddish brown of the burnt kind [5].

sections.title: What Syme actually wrote
sections.body:
On the chart, umber brown is not defined as a pigment at all. Syme's recipe is color mixing: chesnut brown with a little blackish brown [1]. Chesnut brown, in turn, is the characteristic color of the browns in Werner's series, a deep reddish brown and yellowish brown together [1]. Syme spelled it with one *t*, and Baty keeps his spelling [1].

He gave three things to look at. The animal is the moor buzzard, which Baty identifies as the marsh harrier; the plant is the disk of the rudbeckia, or coneflower; the mineral is an oxide of tin [1][2]. Baty's plates use Gould's *Birds of Great Britain* (1862 to 1873), Saint-Hilaire's *Flore et la pomone françaises* (1828) and Sowerby's *British Mineralogy* (1802 to 1817) for the three [2].

sections.title: The browns around it
sections.body:
Umber brown is number 102, second in a run of browns that starts with deep reddish brown (101) [6]. After it come [[chestnut]] (103), yellowish brown (104), wood brown (105), [[liver-brown]] (106), [[hair-brown]] (107) and [[broccoli-brown]] (108) [6]. The run ends with [[olive-brown]], which Syme also called clove brown, and [[blackish-brown]] [6]. It is the reddest and darkest of the first few, and the one named for a pigment.

The chart stayed in use long after Syme [7]. Baty's key to cuckoo eggs collected by Edgar Percival Chance in 1920 to 1922 matches twenty eggs to Syme numbers, and umber brown, 102, is one of them [7].

sections.title: The swatch is not the tube
sections.body:
The swatch here, `#613936`, is a dark reddish brown, with a lightness of 29 and a chroma of 20 [8]. It is the color our library draws from Werner's aged chart, and it also fits Ridgway's 1912 plate I and block 16 of the 1955 ISCC-NBS system [8]. Maerz and Paul give 1912 as its first recorded date [8]. Its nearest everyday name is [[mahogany]], 8.1 units of color difference away, and it is almost the same as the lake color Victoria Lake, 1.1 units off [8].

It also sits 11.6 units of color difference from the page for the pigment, [[umber]] [8]. A chart name inherits a pigment's word, not its recipe: Syme's color comes from chesnut brown and blackish brown, and any tube of umber, raw or burnt, will differ from it [1][5][8].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
In our archive of 23,781 paintings, a color within six units of this swatch covers at least five per cent of the canvas in 728 works, or 3.1 per cent [9]. It is a Renaissance color in the numbers: 61 of 945 paintings from the 1400s (6.5 per cent, 2.1 times the museums' baseline) and 131 of 2,231 from the 1500s, falling to 166 of 6,394 in the 1600s, below baseline [9]. Inside a painting it is a shadow half the time and a middle tone the rest [9].

The painters who hold it most are Florentines: [[painter:bronzino|Bronzino]] in 7 of his 21 works here, [[painter:pontormo|Pontormo]] in 5 of 13 [9]. Tibetan painting has it in 4 of 47 [9]. The largest covers are Indian works, such as a *Ragamala* page of about 1750 with 59 per cent of its canvas in this brown [9]. The earliest match is dated 1201, but the name's earliest record in our sources is 1821, so that is a look-alike color and not Syme's [8][9]. As always these are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so a match is a look-alike color, not a pigment test [9].

In Google Books the phrase "umber brown" peaks around 1860, is at about a quarter of that height by 1880, and is at a fiftieth of it in the 2000s [10].
